title: A child at Patna
hookLine: Gobind Rai is born in Patna in 1666 and grows up playing at archery by the Ganges

cards: A big city on the Ganges, far from Punjab, and a little boy who has never met his father.
Somewhere in your family there may be a story about you at three that comes out at every gathering: the broccoli you fed the dog, the summer you only answered to a superhero's name.

Small stories, but they're how a family says: we knew you before you were anyone. Today begins the story of the tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh: warrior, poet, founder of the Khalsa. But first, the child at Patna.

teach.b: Remember day seventy-six: Guru Tegh Bahadur traveled east, leaving his wife, Mata Gujri, in Patna while he went on toward Assam. There, in December 1666, their son was born. They named him Gobind Rai.
His father would not see him for years. So the boy grew up with his mother, his grandmother Mata Nanaki and his uncle Kirpal Chand, among the Sikh families of a big city on a great river.
Sikhs tell a handful of stories about those years, and they're full of play.

teach.h: ARMIES OF CHILDREN BY THE RIVER.
teach.b: He loved to lead the other children in mock battles, split into two armies. He practiced archery by the river.
Tradition says he would shoot small arrows, or toss things, at the women carrying water pots, cracking the pots, and his mother had to replace them. One story is especially tender.

A local raja's wife, Rani Maini, had no children and longed for a son. Tradition says the little boy came into her house, climbed into her lap, calling her mother, and she fed him boiled, salted chickpeas.
At the gurdwara there today, visitors are still given those chickpeas.
In Patna the Sikh community remembers his birthplace with Takht Sri Patna Sahib, one of the five takhts.
Hold onto this picture: a mischievous, warm, sporty boy, loved by a whole neighborhood. Around 1672 he was brought to Punjab, to his father at Anandpur. Everything else comes later.

how: Sikhs celebrate Guru Gobind Singh's birth each year with prayers and processions, and many visit Takht Sri Patna Sahib, the birthplace, and the gurdwara of Rani Maini, where boiled chickpeas are given as prasad.

games.q: you're Rani Maini, with no children of your own. a little boy from the Guru's household climbs into your lap and calls you mother. what do you do?
games.why: tradition says she fed him boiled, salted chickpeas, and her home is now a gurdwara where chickpeas are still given out.

practice: Go back to being small, and let one game you loved come back: tag in the street, pretend kitchens, a ball against a wall, forts of couch cushions.
Remember the place, the other kids, the rules you made up, how completely absorbed you were, and smile if you want to.

wordCard.voice: Patna Sahib. The gurdwara in Patna marking the birthplace of Gobind Rai, the future tenth Guru, who grew up playing at archery by the Ganges.
